name: Schroth method

card.summary: The Schroth method is a scoliosis-specific physiotherapy system of rotational breathing, posture and muscle exercises that some people use to even out a curved spine, shoulder and trunk asymmetry and so improve how their posture and torso look.
card.note: Developed and studied for diagnosed idiopathic scoliosis and usually taught by trained physiotherapists; it is not a height-gain programme.

quick.overview:
The Schroth method is a physiotherapy approach created in Germany for people with scoliosis, a sideways and rotated curve of the spine. It trains the body to pull the spine, ribcage and pelvis toward a more symmetrical position, which can change how level the shoulders, waist and trunk look.

On looksmaxxing forums it appears in posture and 'bonehacks' discussions, where some users hope that straightening the spine adds a little standing height or evens out the torso. Randomised trials and several meta-analyses in adolescents with idiopathic scoliosis report reductions in Cobb angle (the curve measurement) and trunk rotation compared with standard care or no exercise.
quick.how: The method is normally taught by a trained physiotherapist who analyses the individual curve pattern and builds a personalised set of exercises. These combine postural elongation, rotational breathing into the collapsed side of the ribcage, and holding the corrected position with muscle activity. Trials have used supervised sessions over several weeks or months with home practice, and some programmes run as intensive in-patient courses. It is sometimes used alongside bracing.
quick.risks: Exercise-based scoliosis therapy is generally described as low risk. Poorly matched exercises may cause soreness, and scoliosis needs a clinical diagnosis, since a curve can progress during growth and may need bracing or other care. The method addresses spinal curvature and is not described in the literature as a way to gain height beyond the small amount a straighter spine can reveal.

lead: The Schroth method is a form of physiotherapeutic scoliosis-specific exercise (PSSE) developed by the German teacher and gymnast Katharina Schroth (1894-1985), who had scoliosis herself.[1] It combines three-dimensional postural correction, rotational breathing and muscle-symmetry exercises, with the stated aim of de-rotating, lengthening and stabilising the spine.[1][2]

In appearance terms, the method is used to reduce the curve and rotation that make the shoulders, waist, ribcage and hips look uneven, and to improve posture. People in posture and height communities sometimes cite it because a straighter spine can add a small amount of measured height, though the clinical literature measures outcomes in Cobb angle, angle of trunk rotation and quality of life.[3][4]

Randomised trials and meta-analyses in adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) report that Schroth exercises reduce Cobb angle and trunk rotation relative to comparison care, with effect sizes ranging from moderate to large.[3][4][5] Network meta-analyses compare Schroth with other PSSE schools such as SEAS, DoboMed, FITS and side-shift.[6][7]

angle.text: The Schroth method trains the spine, ribcage and pelvis toward a more symmetrical position. In people with scoliosis this can lessen visible shoulder, rib and waist asymmetry and improve standing posture. Some forum users also mention small height gains from a straighter spine.

Cobb angle, angle of trunk rotation, quality of life

paras: Schroth treatment starts from the idea that scoliosis is a three-dimensional deformity, so correction has to address side-bending, rotation and sagittal alignment together. A therapist classifies the individual curve pattern and teaches corrections specific to it.[2][8]

Exercises typically combine sensorimotor and postural training with corrective breathing that directs air into the concave, collapsed regions of the ribcage, intended to help derotate the trunk.[4] A 2016 review of seven PSSE schools describes Schroth as one of the longest established of these approaches.[8]

Katharina Schroth was born with moderate scoliosis, was fitted with a steel brace at 16 and, dissatisfied with it, experimented on herself with mirrors, breathing techniques and a pulley system.[1] In 1921 she opened a breathing-orthopaedic institute in Meissen with her husband, Franz, and in 1955 she moved to West Germany and founded an institute in Sobernheim, later called the Katharina Schroth Klinik.[1]

Her daughter Christa Lehnert-Schroth directed the Sobernheim institute until 1995, and her grandson Hans-Rudolf Weiss, a physician, continued the work.[1] Schroth is now one of several PSSE schools used in Europe alongside SEAS, BSPTS, FED, FITS, Lyon, Side Shift and DoboMed.[9]

sections.h: Use in looksmaxxing and posture communities
paras: In posture and height discussions, Schroth-type exercises are brought up by people with scoliosis or visible trunk asymmetry who want a more even torso, and by some who hope that straightening a curve will add standing height. The exercises are generally presented as therapy for a diagnosed curve, taught individually.

A 2022 meta-analysis of ten randomised controlled trials in idiopathic scoliosis reported effect sizes from nearly moderate to large for Cobb angle, angle of trunk rotation and quality of life.[3] A 2023 meta-analysis restricted to Schroth used alone in adolescents examined the same three outcomes against no intervention or other conservative treatment.[4] An earlier 2018 meta-analysis pooled 15 primary studies.[10]

A 2024 network meta-analysis of 17 randomised trials (857 patients) found physiotherapeutic scoliosis-specific exercise improved Cobb angle, trunk rotation and quality of life compared with conventional rehabilitation, and compared Schroth-based approaches with other methods.[6] A separate 2024 network meta-analysis of 24 studies (1,069 participants) compared six exercise schools.[7]

Individual trials include a 2016 assessor-blinded randomised trial adding Schroth exercises to standard care in adolescents,[11] a 2021 single-blind trial comparing Schroth with core exercises in 28 adolescents with mild curves,[12] a 12-month supervised programme trial published in 2024,[13] and a 2024 trial combining pelvic rotation correction with Schroth.[14] A 2024 secondary analysis examined posture using surface topography.[15] A 2022 review concluded that growing evidence supports PSSE as a conservative option alongside bracing.[9]

The trials above report exercise outcomes rather than serious adverse events. Because scoliosis can progress during growth, clinicians monitor curves with radiographs and may combine exercise with bracing.[9]
